paragraphs.text: The subject of his writing was hatred of his brothers, and its cause was jealousy and envy, the very things that have hurled countless others into the depths of evil. Jealousy and envy, after all, brought about the murder of a brother at the very beginning. Starting from there, the man wrote this one treatise and no other (would that he had never written it!), and from the very outset set himself to make war on the holy ministers of God. He left aside speaking and writing against the great and numerous throng of heretics who are ravaging his own country, which is exactly what he ought to have done above all (if he had any power of saving speech): like a good shepherd, he should have been driving off the enemies of the church of God among the Galatian people as if they were wolves and wild beasts.

Instead he neglected his own country, as if it were a wasteland teeming with venomous reptiles, and, boiling over idly and to no purpose, let loose his anger on the ministers of God. And not on just any of them, but on those who by the grace of God are conspicuous to all for their way of life and their philosophic conduct; not only on the living, but also on those who have fallen asleep in Christ; and of these, on the very ones whose fame, above all for the virtue of their piety and their training in the divine words, is sung, so to speak, throughout the whole world. These same men he mentioned with abuse not once but many times and in various ways, unsparingly heaping slanders and false accusations on them.

He has even resorted to curses against them, like women in a brawl, reviling and cursing men who had done him no wrong. That is why his writing has run on beyond all due measure to a great and immoderate length, so that a single book was filled out with nearly ten thousand lines.

Naturally, then, having sharpened an abusive tongue against the holy ministers of God and having first practised irreverence and fearlessness on them, he went on next to advance to the very summit of all things, subjecting the only-begotten and beloved Son of God to such godless blasphemies. What sort of blasphemies they are, it is better to hear a little later from his own mouth rather than from mine.

In setting out his own words I shall, for the present, stop at that, without adding long arguments to oppose and refute them, since the men he has blasphemed are not unknown or obscure persons, but are known to all even if I say nothing,

nor is his blasphemy against the Christ of God a disputed or unfamiliar matter that would need great and more closely reasoned effort to refute. The empty babble of this strange new theologian has become so evident, merely by being stated, to all who share in the grace of the church, small and great alike. I shall therefore use only brief annotations, giving the discussion a body by following sequence and order, and merely pointing out the absurdity of what he puts forward.

But before I proceed to his words, I must advise those who read the man's treatise, especially any who are Galatians, not to forget the divine voice of Paul the apostle. Writing to the Galatians themselves, he urged them not to turn away "from him who called" them "in the grace of Christ to another gospel" ("which is not" another, as he said, "only there are some who trouble" them "and want to pervert the gospel of Christ"),

and they must also pay attention to the words in which that great apostle, laying hold even of himself in order to shame those who were trying to pervert these people, went on to say: "But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed."

He repeats this a second time, saying: "As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed." And what was this, against which it was not permitted to preach another gospel, if not surely that very thing which the Savior is recorded to have handed on to his disciples when he said: "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit"?

For he alone has given us this grace of the knowledge of the Holy Trinity through the mystical rebirth; neither Moses nor any of the prophets ministered it to the former people. It befitted the Son of God alone to proclaim the Father's grace to all people, since "the law was given through Moses," but "grace and truth" came through "Jesus Christ" alone, that is, through Jesus as the "only-begotten Son."

Hence, fittingly, Moses, in the manner of a tutor, handed on to the former people, who were still infants, "the elementary principles of the oracles of God," keeping them back from the error of many gods and proclaiming that they should know one God only. But the saving grace, which grants us a knowledge above this world, an angelic knowledge, openly unveiled the mystery that had long been kept in silence from the former people. It proclaimed that the very God who is beyond all things, the God known to the people of old, is God and at the same time Father of the only-begotten Son; and it supplies to the worthy the power of the Holy Spirit through the Son.

From that source, so to speak, the church of God has received the holy, blessed and mystical Trinity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit for the hope of salvation through rebirth in Christ, and guards it. And this was the gospel which it is not lawful to exchange for another gospel, "which is not another," as the great apostle bears witness to the Galatians even to this day, crying out through his epistle to them: "Even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you contrary to what you received, let him be accursed." Long beforehand, it seems, he was warning them not to heed even bishops or rulers or teachers, if any of them should pervert the true word of the faith.

And what was this gospel, if not the one that teaches us to know God the Father, hands down to us the knowledge of the Son of God, and bids us strive eagerly to share in the Holy Spirit? These would be the marks of Christians alone, and in this way the holy church of God is set apart from the Jewish way.

For as the Jewish way rejected the polytheistic error of the Greeks by confessing one God, so the church's special knowledge concerning the Son has brought about something better and greater, teaching us to know the same God as Father of an only-begotten Son, who is truly a Son, living and subsisting. "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself," the only-begotten of God himself taught us, saying this,

so that the Father may be truly Father (not merely so called in word, nor holding a false title, but Father of an only-begotten Son in truth and in fact), and the Son truly Son. But anyone who supposes the Son to be a mere word, who protests that he is only a word, and who says again and again that he was nothing other than a word, remaining within the Father while the Father is at rest but active when he creates the creation, just like our own word, which is at rest when we are silent but active when we speak, would plainly be falling in with a Jewish and human way of thinking and denying the true Son of God.

If, for instance, someone were to ask one of the Jews whether God has a word, he will certainly say yes, since every Jew would confess that God has a word, and indeed many words. But that he also has a Son, he would no longer confess if asked.

And if it is not one of the Jews but one of the bishops who introduces this opinion, granting him only a Word united with God, and saying that this Word is everlasting and unbegotten and is one and the same with God, called by the different names of Father and Son but one in essence and hypostasis, how could he fail to be shown up as slipping into the role of Sabellius and as estranged from the knowledge and grace that are in Christ? For the ordinance of the church would not permit them to inquire, doubt or ask whether the only-begotten Son of God existed and pre-existed. Rather, with an acknowledged and undoubted faith, and with great confidence and boldness, it teaches us to confess that God is the Father of the only-begotten Son, and not to think that the Father is the Son or the Son the Father; but to revere the one as the unbegotten, everlasting, beginningless, first and only Father, and to believe that the other was begotten from the Father and subsists and is the one only-begotten Son, and to acknowledge him as God, since he is truly the Son of God.

If, then, anyone should be seen to contradict these things and to define the Word of God as being like the word in human beings, how could he fail to be convicted of neither understanding nor considering that nothing mortal or human must be attributed to the God who is beyond all things, nor anything at all that arises in our thoughts? This holds even though the divine scriptures, tutoring their readers as if they were infants, speak of him in rather human terms, attaching to him hands and feet and eyes and voices and words and a mouth and a face and countless other such things. These must be transferred to conceptions worthy of God, without imagining anything mortal or human in God. For "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth," as the Savior himself taught.

And if he is spirit, clearly he is divine spirit, superior to every perceptible and composite body, so that he has neither a perceptible word, sounded out by a tongue and heard by mortal ears through utterance, nor a tongue nor a voice nor a face nor anything else that can be compared with mortal and human reasoning.

For if the divine apostle taught that the things "which God has prepared for those who love him" are such as "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man," then the giver of all these ineffable things must himself be more ineffable than all of them. So it would be far truer to say, in theology about him, that eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has the knowledge that would comprehend him entered "into the heart of men."

The same argument would apply to the begetting of the Son. In these matters the Savior himself would be a worthy hierophant for us, when he says: "All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son."

Suppose, then, that someone should speak against these things and not dare to say that the Son, to whom the Father handed over all things, subsists, but define him only as a word like the word in human beings: at one time at rest in God, like ours when we are silent, at another time active, much like ours when it is uttered in speaking. Suppose he should then say that at a certain moment, not even four hundred full years ago, this very word took on flesh (how, I do not know) and through it accomplished the economy in human form, and only then became Son of God, was called Jesus Christ, was proclaimed king, and was shown to be the image "of the invisible God" and the firstborn "of all creation," when he had never been so before. Suppose that, on top of such absurdity, he should not grant Christ life and kingdom unending and without limit even from the time he himself proposed, but should impose on him an end that is neither auspicious nor like that of those who will be counted worthy, through him, of the promises the Savior himself has made, when he pledged eternal life and incorruption, immortality and the kingdom of heaven to those who love him;

and suppose he should claim that, when the hoped-for fulfilment of these things arrives, the blessings of the kingdom will endure for all others for an endless age, but that Christ alone will be stripped of all of them at once: his kingdom will cease, the flesh he took on will be left deserted, and the Word itself, which pre-existed in God, will be separated from the body (even though that body be immortal and incorruptible) and joined to God, so as to become one and the same with God once again, just as it was before. What excess of impiety would such a man fall short of?

That is why the testimony of the apostle's warning is needed against such people, when it says: "Even if an angel from heaven should preach contrary to what you received, let him be accursed." And as I consider the apostle's mind, I am moved to wonder. For as though prophesying the future, he set out the theology of the Savior with precision for the Galatians themselves, writing right at the beginning of his epistle to them in a more novel way than was his custom: "Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ."

One would not find him writing this way to anyone else, presumably because none of the others to whom he wrote held such views about the faith. For he was bringing correction to people who supposed Christ to be a mere man, teaching them at the beginning of the epistle that he was not a man. And going on, he said to the same people: "The gospel of mine that was preached to you is not according to man; I did not receive it from a man, nor was I taught it, but it came through a revelation of Jesus Christ." By these words he showed once again that Jesus Christ was not a man.

What he was, if not a man, he made clear further on, saying: "But when God, who set me apart from my mother's womb, was pleased to reveal his Son in me." You see how plainly he proclaimed the Savior to be Son of God, and therefore God.

And that he knew him to be Son of God before his coming in the flesh, he shows most clearly when he adds in the same epistle to the Galatians: "But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of a woman." So it was not now, but before he was born of a woman, that the Father sent him, already being Son and pre-existing, so that he who had long been Son of God might also become Son of man, being born "of a woman."

He also teaches that the Son became mediator of the law of Moses, defining the meaning of that mediation when he says: "Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one." You hear how in these words the apostle taught the Galatians themselves, even then, to know the one God, and the one mediator between God and the angels.

He made this plain elsewhere too, saying: "For God is one; one also is the mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ." But when he named him mediator "between God and men," he fittingly called him a man because of his becoming man; whereas when he presented the same one as mediator not between God and men but between God and angels, he no longer named him a man, but calls him only mediator, saying that the law was ordained "through angels by the hand of a mediator,"

and he necessarily clarifies the term "mediator" by drawing a distinction, when he says: "Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one." So God would not be the mediator (for of whom could he be mediator?), nor would the mediator himself be that one God; for "a mediator is not of one."

He stands, then, between two. Which two these are, he makes clear by naming the angels and God. The Son of God, being between them, received the law, he says, with his own hand from the Father, and ordained it "through angels" for the first people. So from that time the Son was mediator between God and the angels, before he became "mediator between God and men."

And he existed not as a mere word of God, without subsistence, one and the same with God (for in that case he would not be a mediator at all), but he existed and pre-existed as the "only-begotten Son, full of grace and truth." And he was acting as mediator for the Father, who was giving the law to human beings "through angels." Teaching this even then to those who were ignorant and untaught in the theology of the Son of God, the apostle set his seal on it by saying: "Now a mediator is not of one." For it is not in the nature of a mediator to be defined in relation to one alone.

Therefore he is not of one, but is of necessity between two, being neither of the two between whom he stands. So when he mediates between the Father and the angels, we must regard him neither as the God over all himself nor as one of the angels, but as standing between them as mediator. Just so, in turn, when he becomes "mediator between God and men," standing between both orders, he is neither of those between whom he mediates: he is neither himself the one and only God, nor a man in the same way as the rest of men.

What, then, if none of these, is he but the only-begotten Son of God, who has now become mediator between men and God, but who long ago, in the time of Moses, was mediator between God and the angels? Writing these things to them, the great apostle hands them on in these words: "The law, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator.

Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one." So "God" is "one," and there is "one mediator" between "God" and all things that have come into being, who did not begin his saving mediation only now, but was mediator even before his divine appearing among men, as the argument has shown.

These points have now been briefly set out for the Galatians from their own epistle alone. The saving faith provides the mystical rebirth "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," and the catholic church of God, from the ends of the earth to the ends of the earth, sets its seal by unwritten tradition, alongside the divine writings, on the testimonies drawn from the divine scriptures. So it is time now to examine the words of Marcellus and to furnish proofs of what we have promised, so that no one may think the man is being slandered by us.

Since my aim is to set out briefly what he has said, I shall not collect all the man's words, but shall use only the essential ones, passing over most of them as superfluous and as covering the same ground. But before demonstrating what he has said, I think I must first show readers that he did not examine with care even the plain words of the divine readings, so that those who still do not know him may learn what sort of man he was who was led to such audacity in what he said.

To take an immediate example: the prophet Zechariah, who lived at the time of the return from Babylon, mentioned Joshua the high priest, that is, the son of Jozadak, who together with Zerubbabel led those returning from Babylon. Our noble and admirable author, unaware of this, cites the passage of Zechariah in which Joshua is mentioned, but, flung far wide of the history, he has supposed that the prophet is speaking of Joshua, the successor of Moses.

Again, when the apostle wrote in the Epistle to the Galatians in this way, "But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother," he either forgot, or did not understand, or even deliberately distorted the saying, writing: "But our Jerusalem is above; for she is in slavery with her children."

And again, when our Savior said to Peter, "Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, because you are not minding the things of God but the things of men," he failed to grasp how and for what reason the saying was addressed to the apostle, and claims that these words were spoken to the devil. He puts all these errors together in a single passage, writing word for word as follows: "That no name among those named on earth has been greater than that of Jesus is attested by the Gospel, where the angel said to Mary, 'Do not be afraid, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.

He will be great, and will be called Son of the Most High.' It is clear too from the prophecy of Zechariah, which long ago prophesied concerning this name: 'The Lord showed me,' he says, 'Jesus the great priest, standing before the face of the angel of the Lord. And the devil stood at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to the devil: May the Lord who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you.'

"For when did he rebuke him? When he joined to his own Word the man he loved. 'He who has chosen Jerusalem,' he says, meaning plainly this Jerusalem of ours, concerning which the apostle says, 'But our Jerusalem is above; for she is in slavery with her children.'

"For it was then, when he had come into this great Jerusalem, that is, into our Church, that he rebuked the devil in accordance with the prophecy, saying, 'Go away behind me, Satan, for you are a stumbling block to me.' This, then, is the great priest, of whom the Jesus of that time preserved the type.

"For it was not possible for that man to be called a great priest, glorious though he was in all things, when Moses was not called great (for Moses was not yet great, since he was called a servant of God, and was named a god to Pharaoh by God himself).

"But if anyone should think that Jesus was called great on the ground that he was deemed worthy to lead the people into the holy land and did many other wonders, let him learn from this too that the greatness spoken of in the case of Jesus pertained not so much to the typological event as to the one who a little later was to lead his own people into this great Jerusalem." You see how ignorant he was, having strayed from the history and having been unable to attend to the Jesus referred to by the prophet Zechariah.

For that man was the son of Jozadak, of the tribe of the Levites, who had received the high priesthood as a descendant of Aaron, which is why he was also styled great priest, just as the prophet teaches when he says, "And the Lord showed me Jesus the great priest."

But the successor of Moses, the one who led the people into the land of promise and did many other wonderful things, was the son of Nun, and of the tribe of Ephraim, which had nothing to do with the priesthood. How, then, could a man who has so badly missed the plain wording, and who is ignorant of the bare history, be competent to teach the highest theology? Likewise in the case of Peter one ought to have considered how the words "Get behind me" were spoken to him,

and what the meaning of the name Satan is, and why he also called him a "stumbling block," and how at almost one and the same time both "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah" and "Get behind me, Satan" were said to him,

and what is meant by "going behind" the Savior (which he himself explained on the spot, adding immediately, "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me"; which Peter himself indeed carried out in deed a little later, when he was perfected by martyrdom);

and one ought also to have inquired for what things he called him blessed, and for what he rebuked him. But he, paying attention to none of these things, declared, contrary to Scripture, that these words were spoken to the devil.

Is this, then, the only thing he did not know? Does he not, going on further, after mentioning the resurrection of our Savior and then wishing to show that even before him, in the times of the prophets, someone is recorded as having been raised from the dead, go wrong here too, saying that the prophet Elisha was the first to raise someone from the dead? He did not know that even before Elisha the great Elijah raised up the widow's son who had died, as can be learned from 1 Kings.

He is evidently ignorant of this too, as appears from his writing as follows: "Not only, then, does the apostle say that he is the firstborn of the 'new creation,' but also the firstborn 'from the dead,' for no other reason, in my view, than that through his being firstborn 'of the dead' it might be possible to understand in what sense he is also called 'firstborn of all creation.' For our Lord Jesus Christ was not the first to rise from the dead; the one who rose through Elisha the prophet rose earlier, and Lazarus too rose before his resurrection, and at the time of the passion 'many bodies of those who had fallen asleep' rose."

This too Marcellus seems to me to have set down without reflection, I mean that "many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep" were raised before him. For he did not attend to the whole passage of the Gospel, which teaches that the bodies of the saints were raised "after his resurrection."

You will find him going wrong also in his exposition of a saying of the apostle. For the divine apostle, writing to the Romans, says this: "set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was declared Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness."

But he, with what intention I do not know, distorts the apostle's wording here as well, making "declared" into "predestined," so that he might be like those who were predestined "according to foreknowledge."

He says, word for word, as follows: "Just as, then, Almighty God long ago predestined the Church, so too he predestined the dispensation of Christ according to the flesh, through whom he predestined to call the race of the godly 'to adoption,' having first laid its foundation in his own mind. For this reason the apostle, by the Holy Spirit, clearly proclaims it beforehand, saying, 'of the Son of God who was predestined.'" And again he says elsewhere: "This is he of whom Paul said, 'of the Son of God who was predestined.'"

Here too he has corrupted not only the apostle's wording but the very sense, by adding the preposition "pre-." And doing things akin to these, when the psalm reads, "From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you," he here too makes use of an addition that is found nowhere in the text, in order to find fault with one who does not speak as he does.
Listen, then, to how he writes, saying: "For this reason, then, it seems good to me now to go through also the things I have not yet gone through before.

"For most of what he wrote has been made clear by what we have already said. 'From the womb,' he says, 'before the morning star I begot you forth.' For he surely thought that, if the preposition 'forth' were stolen away, the text would fall in with the opinion of his heresy. Therefore, by removing the most essential part of the word, he wished to make it signify his ancient regeneration." And since in these words he has argued vigorously for his own error, faulting the one who wrote correctly while himself saying nothing to prove it, he hands his readers testimony to that very reading.

Going on further, the same man introduces the Savior as saying, "I am the day," putting it something like this: "For since there was darkness before, through ignorance of true religion, and the day was about to appear ('for I am,' he says, 'the day'), he fittingly calls the star the morning star."

And in another place he says: "Since after the assumption of the flesh he is proclaimed both Christ and Jesus, and life and way and day." And again, going further, he cites the apostle's saying, "But our Jerusalem is above."

But why need I go on at length, when anyone who wishes can, on the basis of what has been said, gather similar examples from the whole treatise and observe the man's carelessness? Out of this carelessness you will hear him frequently calling Solomon a prophet and naming the Proverbs prophecies;

as, for instance, where he says: "For this reason the most holy prophet Solomon said, 'to receive the twists of words,'" and again, "'sayings of the wise and riddles'" — he calls the proverb a prophecy — and again: "Therefore it seems to me that this most wise prophet also spoke the first words of the prophecy in the manner of proverbs."

And he does this a second and third time and often, as I said, not knowing that "there are varieties of gifts," even if there is "the same Spirit," and that to one "is given the word of wisdom," according to the apostle, "to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another prophecies." Accordingly, Solomon is attested to have received the gift of wisdom:

"For the Lord gave Solomon wisdom," as Scripture says, "and he became wiser than all men"; but he neither led the life of a prophet nor displays in his own words the character of prophecy, which is recognized by "Thus says the Lord" and similar expressions.

But he, perceiving none of this, calls him a prophet as though doing the man a favor, not understanding that the prophets "went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, destitute, afflicted, ill-treated." And he says that his Proverbs are prophecy, though divine Scripture nowhere teaches this, and the most wise man himself, with the divine Spirit, gave this book the name PROVERBS, the second ECCLESIASTES, and the third SONG OF SONGS,

bestowing these titles not without God nor by human reasoning. Moreover, he tries to interpret his divinely inspired writing by means of Greek examples, not heeding the apostle Paul when he says: "We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God, so that we may know the things freely given to us by God; which things we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Holy Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him; and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned." Ignorant of this too, our noble friend tries to set before us the meaning of the divine Proverbs from Greek reading, writing in these very words as follows:

"For there is nothing out of place, I think, in reminding you at present of a few proverbs from outside. 'EITHER HE IS DEAD OR HE IS TEACHING LETTERS.' Judging by the surface of the wording, one might suppose this proverb was said against those who teach letters, since another of their writers also said, 'You taught letters, and I attended school.' But those who wrote the commentaries said that this is not so; rather, they say, when the Sicilians defeated the Athenians in war, they spared only those who claimed to be educated, taking them as teachers for their children, and killed all the rest. When some of these escaped and returned home and were asked by the Athenians about certain people dear to them, they are said to have replied, 'EITHER HE IS DEAD OR HE IS TEACHING LETTERS.'

"And what about 'THE GOAT AND THE KNIFE'? One might think — to set down first what is said about it — that the proverb was surely said because the goat being sacrificed looks at the knife. But this is not at all what the ancients said; for what was said would not even be a proverb if that were the case (for this is what one would naturally gather from the surface meaning). Rather, they say it is said of those who bring evils upon themselves. For they say that Medea, having killed her children in Corinth, hid the knife there; and that the Corinthians, when offering a black goat in accordance with an oracle given them, were at a loss for a knife, and the goat, scraping with its foot, discovered Medea's knife and was sacrificed with it.

"And what does 'ENOUGH OF THE OAK' mean? someone asks; for the proverb cannot be understood from its surface. The ancients, as they say, ate acorns before wheat was cultivated; and since, as they thought, this grain was discovered later, they turned their attention to it and, rejoicing at the change, said, 'ENOUGH OF THE OAK'; and this, they said, is the proverb.

"And again, since another proverb has been cited by very many of their wise men in very many different books, it is necessary at present to mention what those who undertook to interpret the proverbs have written about it, [?] but in order to refute Asterius, who knows precisely from secular learning too what is peculiar to a proverb, yet at present has feigned ignorance, so that he might seem to establish his own intention plausibly by using the proverbial saying. It is 'GLAUCUS'S ART.' The wise men outside, mentioning this proverb, explained it in different ways.

"One of them said that a certain Glaucus, who was master of a certain art, the most marvelous of many [?], perished at sea, and the art with him, before anyone had learned it from him. Another, attesting that Glaucus had the highest skill in music, speaks of four bronze disks made by him for producing, when struck, a melodious harmony of sounds; and that the proverb was said from this.

"Another says that among the offerings of Alyattes there was dedicated a mixing bowl and a marvelous stand, the work of Glaucus of Chios. Another, that Glaucus himself dedicated at Delphi a bronze tripod, so crafted that [?] when it was struck heavily, the feet on which it stood, the upper casing, the rim on the cauldron, and the rods set through the middle sounded with the voice of a lyre. And again another says the proverb was said from a certain Glaucus who was thought to have achieved something beyond the ordinary.

"You see how the difficulty of the proverb is shown by this as well, by the fact that those who wished to explain this proverb did not settle on the same interpretation. So hard to discover does the matter of the proverb seem to be even among those outside. For this reason one of their wise men, collecting the proverbs that had been spoken by many in various ways, wrote six books on them, two on those in verse and four on those in prose.

"Those outside called these proverbs for no other reason, in my view, than that, having come upon the Proverbs of the most wise Solomon and learned from them that nothing said in them can be clearly understood from the surface, they too, wishing to emulate the prophetic writing, wrote in the same manner as he did. Then, being unable to think of any name more fitting than that, they called these proverbs too."

With such citations Marcellus tries to teach the Church of God to understand the divinely inspired Scriptures. I have quoted this whole long and garrulous rigmarole wishing to show the folly of the great and ill-timed ambition the man indulges in, making a display of Greek learning while forgetting the divine words.

For he would never have fallen into such nonsense if he had remembered the apostolic precepts, in which the apostle urges that "the things freely given to us by God" must be spoken "not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual,"

nor if he had understood how it was said that "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned." Ignorant of this, he supposed that the wise men of the Greeks had gained knowledge of the wisdom bestowed by God on Solomon and, having known it, emulated the prophetic writing, as he puts it.

And how could they be capable of knowing and emulating divine things, being natural men and not knowing how to compare "spiritual things with spiritual," when the divine apostle has declared that "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God"? When the same apostle said that the natural man cannot know spiritual things, "because they are spiritually discerned," our noble friend, holding the contrary opinion to the apostle, asserts that those who composed the Greek proverbs wrote in the same manner as Solomon.

For he says, word for word: "since, having come upon the Proverbs of the most wise Solomon and learned from them that nothing said in them can be clearly understood from the surface, they too, wishing to emulate the prophetic writing, wrote in the same manner as he did." But consider in another way too, from the citations themselves, how far he has strayed from the truth in saying that the Greek writers wrote in the same manner as Solomon.

For Solomon, moved by God-given wisdom, devoted his entire writing to the word of true religion for the benefit and salvation of souls, and to exercise the minds of his readers he used obscure problems, twists of words, and sayings put forward in riddles. He attests this at the beginning of the book, saying: "For when a wise man hears these things he will become wiser, and the man of understanding will acquire guidance, and will understand a parable and dark words, the sayings of the wise and riddles,"

and again, "to receive the twists of words." That this is so is easy to learn from the contents of the book, which cannot be understood otherwise than by our passing from the surface wording to the meaning discerned through it; for example: "The leech had three daughters, dearly beloved, and these three did not satisfy her, and the fourth was not content to say, 'Enough,'"

and "Wisdom has built herself a house and set up seven pillars; she has slaughtered her sacrifices, she has mixed her wine in a bowl," and all other such sayings, which cannot be understood in any other way, neither from the surface nor from any history, but only through metaphor and a turning of the wording. But the Greek proverbs that he set out took their origins from certain stories.

For "EITHER HE IS DEAD OR HE IS TEACHING LETTERS" was said, he says, because of a certain story, and "THE GOAT AND THE KNIFE" was said because of another such event; and "ENOUGH OF THE OAK" likewise, because people who once ate acorns gave up that kind of food. And if a certain Glaucus, who was master of some art, was recorded in different ways by later writers who disagreed in their accounts of him, what has that to do with the divinely inspired Proverbs? For these do not, like the Greek proverbs, find their solution in some story. Ignorantly, then, and without experience of the contemplation of the divine Scriptures — and not only that, but contrary to the apostle — Marcellus has declared that the wise men of the Greeks, having come upon the Proverbs of Solomon, learned and emulated the prophetic writing and wrote in the same manner as he did.

Now that we have said these things to prove that the man has not read even the divine Scriptures in the way he ought, the time has come to examine also the unsound opinion of his faith, since, holding views contrary to the Church's teaching, he has slandered both the Church and those who preside over her.

First I will set out the passages in which he tries to contradict what was written correctly and in keeping with the Church, slandering those who wrote it and all but staging a free-for-all fight against everyone. At one moment he aims his rebuttal at Asterius, at another at the great Eusebius.

Then he turns on the man of God, the truly thrice-blessed Paulinus. Paulinus was honored with the rank of presbyter in the church of Antioch and served with distinction as bishop of Tyre, and he shone so brightly in that office that the church of Antioch claimed him as its own treasure.

Yet this admirable writer mocks even him, a man who lived a blessed life, rested in blessedness, fell asleep long ago, and never troubled him at all. Passing on from him, he wages war on Origen, who also departed this life long ago. Then he marches against Narcissus and hounds the other Eusebius. At the same time he rejects all the fathers of the Church, being pleased with no one at all except himself alone.

He writes, then, maligning them all by name, as follows: "I will begin, then, with the letter he wrote, and answer each of the things that were not written rightly. He has written that he believes in God the Father Almighty, and in his Son, the only-begotten God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit; and he says that he learned this way of piety from the divine Scriptures.

For my part, when he says this, I wholeheartedly accept what is said, for this way of piety is common to all of us: to believe in Father and Son and Holy Spirit. But when, without having grasped the divine power, he speaks to us in too human a way, through some artful speculation, calling the Father a father and the Son a son, I no longer consider it safe to praise such speculation.

For it is through such speculation that the heresy now being devised by them comes to grow, as I think is easy to show clearly from his own words. For he said that one must hold that the Father is truly a father, and the Son truly a son, and the Holy Spirit likewise."

So writes Marcellus against Asterius. He is displeased that one should confess that the Father is truly a father, and the Son truly a son, and the Holy Spirit likewise. In what follows, therefore, he tries at greater length to overturn the argument on these matters. For he wants to confess that Christ is a mere word, like a human word, and not a Son who truly lives and subsists.

Since he said that this heresy is only now being devised, it must be pointed out that as he goes on he mentions Origen, who lived long ago, as sharing the views of those he is now slandering. I myself, however, have read a great many ecclesiastical writings by men even older than Origen, as well as various letters of bishops and synods written long ago, and they show one and the same stamp of the faith.

So he was wrong to slander them by saying that this heresy is now being devised by the men he maligns. A little further on he reviles not only Asterius but also the great Eusebius, whose episcopate very many illustrious provinces and cities sought to claim. He does so in this way: "I will remind you of what he himself wrote in support of the things badly written by Eusebius, so that you may see that he clearly departs from his earlier profession.

For he has written in these very words: 'The main point of the letter is to refer the generation of the Son to the will of the Father, and not to declare the begetting a passion of God. This is what the wisest of the fathers declared in their own treatises, guarding against the impiety of the heretics, who falsely attributed to God a bodily and passible begetting of offspring by teaching emanations.'"

Against these words too he makes a long rebuttal in what follows, after which he adds: "So Asterius, wishing to defend Eusebius, who wrote badly, mentioned the nature of the Father and the nature of the unbegotten, and so became his own accuser. It would have been far better to leave the depth of Eusebius's thought unexamined, lying in the brevity in which he wrote it, than to apply such speculation and bring the craftiness of the writing to light."

After other things he adds: "But now let us examine one particular statement among those written by Asterius. He said: 'For the Father, who begot from himself the only-begotten Word and firstborn of all creation, is one.' He has put both together, writing 'only-begotten' and 'firstborn,' although these names greatly contradict each other, as even the very slowest learners can easily see.

For it is clear that the only-begotten, if he were truly only-begotten, can no longer be firstborn, and the firstborn, insofar as he is firstborn, cannot be only-begotten." Here too he blames Asterius in vain. The words that call the Son of God at one time the only-begotten Son and at another the firstborn of all creation were not Asterius's but those of divine Scripture.

Again he adds to these, saying: "But abandoning true knowledge, he has once more displayed his artful speculation to us. Unable to establish his own intention from the divine Scriptures, he runs back to the fathers he supposes to be 'wisest,' saying: 'This is what the wisest of the fathers declared in their own treatises.'
Asterius says that his own fathers made a pronouncement and wrote a dogma about God according to their own choice. For the word 'dogma' belongs to human will and opinion.

That this is so is amply attested by the dogmatic art of the physicians, and attested also by the so-called dogmas of the philosophers. And I think no one is unaware that what the Senate has resolved is still called even now the 'dogmas' of the Senate." Marcellus was led to say this too, forgetting the apostolic saying about the Savior, "having abolished the law of commandments in dogmas." What is more, he finds fault with the duty of following the fathers, although divine Scripture says, "Ask your father, and he will declare it to you;

your elders, and they will tell you," and "Do not move the eternal boundaries that your fathers set." Then, indignant that Asterius called Paulinus blessed, and again speaking ill of Eusebius at the same time, he writes as follows: "Wishing to defend Eusebius, who wrote the letter badly, he said first that Eusebius composed the letter without unfolding the doctrine in the manner of a teacher, since the letter was addressed not to the Church or to the uninstructed but to the blessed Paulinus. He called him blessed for this reason: that he held the same opinion as Asterius. So, since we have learned who Asterius's 'wisest fathers' are, I think it fitting to name also the man who became the teacher of Paulinus and the others.

For the man who became his teacher too would become plain to us from Paulinus's letter." After saying some things in between, he again slanders the same man for having wrongly accepted Origen, speaking thus: "Paulinus wrote this not by recalling the teaching of the Gospel, but by acknowledging that some are moved in this way of themselves, while others have been led in this manner by reading the men mentioned before.

Then finally, adding as it were a crowning flourish to his proof, he appended to his own letter some sayings of Origen, as though Origen could persuade better than the evangelists and the apostles. These are the sayings: 'It is time to take up again the subject of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and to go through a few of the points that were left out before. Concerning the Father: that, being indivisible and without parts, he becomes Father of the Son, not by putting him forth, as some suppose.
For if the Son is something put forth from the Father and an offspring from him, like the offspring of animals, then both the one who puts forth and the one put forth must necessarily be bodies.'"

Then next, after quoting Origen's words, he goes on to say: "Origen wrote these things because he did not wish to learn about the eternity of the Word from the holy prophets and apostles. Instead, giving himself too much licence, he vainly dares to describe a second hypothesis of the Word." He contradicts these things that Origen rightly said, that one must not suppose the generation of the Son's divinity to be bodily and passible, chiefly because Origen gave the Son a real subsistence. And he goes on to speak ill of Origen again and to contradict what Origen rightly wrote, in these words: "That in writing such things Origen was following his own opinions is clear from the fact that he often overturns his own statements. At any rate, it is fitting to recall what he says about God in another passage. He writes thus:

'For God did not begin to be Father after being prevented, as human beings who become fathers are, by not yet being able to be fathers. For if God is always perfect, and the power to be Father is present to him, and it is good for him to be Father of such a Son, why would he put it off and deprive himself of the good, and, so to speak, fail to become Father from the moment he is able to be Father? The same, indeed, must be said about the Holy Spirit as well.'

How then, when Origen had written this too, did Paulinus, whom Asterius calls blessed, think it unsafe to keep this hidden, and yet use statements contrary to it to establish his own opinions? I would say that not even Origen himself could give an account of them." Here Marcellus lied in saying that Origen contradicted himself. He could not understand that by the first quotation Origen was showing that the Father is incorporeal and impassible, and by the second that the Son was begotten not in time but before all ages.

Again, after other things, the same man writes this about Origen: "And yet, if one must tell the truth about Origen, it is fitting to say this. He had only just left the studies of philosophy and chose to devote himself to the divine words before he had an exact grasp of the Scriptures. Because of the abundance and ambition of his secular education, he began to write sooner than he should have, was led astray by the arguments of philosophy, and because of them wrote some things that were not good. This is clear: still mindful of Plato's doctrines

and of the distinction Plato makes among first principles, he wrote a book On First Principles and gave his treatise this title. The greatest proof of this is that he took the opening words, as well as the title of the book, from nowhere else but from the words Plato spoke. For he wrote, beginning thus:

'Those who have believed and been persuaded.' You will find this saying, worded in just this way, in Plato's Gorgias." Even if it were found there, it would bring no reproach on Origen for saying "those who have believed or been persuaded," and adding next that grace and truth came "through Jesus Christ," and that Christ is the truth, according to his own words, "I am the truth." For what fellowship could Plato ever have with these things?

No book of Plato's called On First Principles is recorded, nor did Origen hold views about first principles like Plato's. Origen knew only one first principle, unbegotten, without beginning and beyond all things, and knew that this principle is the Father of one only-begotten Son, through whom all things came to be.

But having lied about Origen here too, after other things he adds: "When Asterius said that the Word was begotten before the ages, the very text refutes him as a liar, so that he misses not only the substance but also the letter. For if Proverbs says, 'Before the age he established me,' how could he himself say that he was begotten before the ages? To have been established before the age is one thing, and to have been begotten before the ages is another."

Having said this, and having added other arguments to overturn the claim that the Son was begotten before the ages, he adds in these very words: "I ask those of the saints who read this, since they have truly received, as it were, the seeds and first principles of this interpretation, to add further proofs to what has been said, so that the intentions of those who pervert the faith may be exposed all the more. For truly they have forsaken God who begot them, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns."

Having hurled such abuse in these words too, he next tries to show that the Son is not even the image of God, speaking thus: "I think it fitting to say a few words about the image as well. For he wrote: 'And another is the one begotten from him, who is the image of the invisible God.' Asterius mentions the image of the invisible God for this reason: to teach that God differs from the Word as much as a man is thought to differ from his own image."

After saying some things in between, he adds: "So it is plain that before he assumed our body the Word by himself was not the image of the invisible God. For an image must be seen, so that through the image what was until then unseen may be seen." And he continues: "How then did Asterius write that the Word of God is the image of the invisible God? For images show the things whose images they are even when these are absent, so that the absent one seems to appear through them.

But if, since God is invisible, the Word turns out to be invisible as well, how can the Word by himself be the image of the invisible God, when he himself is invisible?" Going further, he again heaps abuse on them, saying: "How then do those 'full of deceit and villainy,' to use the Apostle's words, transfer the text to what they suppose was his first creation, when David plainly spoke of his birth according to the flesh?"

Having drawn out a long discourse in between, he adds: "What then will he say to this? I do not think he has anything to say about it. Nor do I think he would openly and without disguise confess to others what he hides in his own mind, as one can clearly learn from what he has written. 'For the Father,' he says, 'is one, who begot from himself the only-begotten Word and firstborn of all creation: one alone begetting one alone, perfect begetting perfect, king begetting king, lord begetting lord, God begetting God, the unvarying image of his essence, will, glory and power.' These words plainly expose his wicked opinion about the Godhead.

For how can the one begotten as Lord and God, as he himself said earlier, be the image of God? An image of God is one thing, and God is another. So if he is an image, he is neither Lord nor God, but the image of the Lord and God; and if he is truly Lord and God, then the Lord and God can no longer be the image of the Lord and God."

He said this too in great blindness. It did not occur to him that a son can sometimes be called a living image of his own father, when he closely resembles his father. Scripture teaches this when it says, "Adam lived two hundred and thirty years, and begot after his own form and after his own image, and he named him Seth."

And concerning the divinity of the Son the Apostle teaches, saying, "who, being in the form of God, did not consider being equal with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself," and again, "who, being the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his substance." Elsewhere too it is said, "For she is the radiance of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness."

Again, when the Apostle says, "having put off the old self and put on the new, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its Creator," he plainly teaches that it is not the flesh that is said to be the image of God.

Passing on again to the bishops, Marcellus writes thus: "See, what grieves us is not so much the matter of Asterius, that he was led to write such things, but that some of those who are thought to preside over the Church have forgotten the apostolic tradition, have preferred what is foreign to the divine teachings, and have dared to write and teach such things, which cling to error no less than those mentioned before."

After other things he adds: "I came upon a letter of Narcissus, who presides over Neronias, which he wrote to a certain Chrestus, Euphronius and Eusebius. Bishop Hosius had asked him whether he too says that there are two essences, as Eusebius of Palestine does, and I learned from what was written that he answered that he believes there are three essences." Having said this, he passes from Narcissus to Eusebius, accusing him of confessing that the Word of God is God.

He writes this about him: "He dared to divide the Word of God and to call the Word another god, separate from the Father in essence and power. How deep a blasphemy he has fallen into can be learned clearly and easily from the very words he wrote.

For he wrote in these very words: 'Surely the image and that of which it is the image are not conceived as one and the same, but as two essences, two things and two powers, just as there are that many names.'" And as though his slander were well aimed, he adds: "How then have these men not turned onto the same evil path as the pagans and set out to teach and write the same things, with Eusebius speaking like Valentinus and Hermes, and Narcissus like Marcion and Plato?"

Next he strings together a long, garrulous and endless babble, claiming to have learned by hearsay that Eusebius once conversed with someone while he was in Laodicea. He writes about things he did not know, as though he had learned them by hearsay, and adds: "On the contrary, he ought to cry out to the Lord with tears and mourning, 'We have sinned, we have acted impiously, we have done wrong,' and 'we have done evil in your sight, and now we repent and beg to receive your loving-kindness.'

This is what would have suited him; this is what it would have profited him to say, given God's boundless goodness and love for humankind. And yet it would have been fitting for God, who cares for us with love and justice, to answer him, saying: 'If an enemy had reproached me, I would have borne it; and if one who hates me had boasted against me, I would have hidden from him. But you, a man of like soul, my guide and my close friend, who shared sweet food with me, we walked together in the house of God in concord.'

We know that he is with us, his ministers, from his own words: 'Behold,' he said, 'I will be with you all the days' of your life 'until the end of the age.' Then he would surely have added, in due order, the words that follow those just quoted: 'Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into Hades, for wickedness is in their hearts.' For Scripture says that those who are dead in the ignorance of impiety are swallowed up by Hades; for even while they seemed to be alive, they were dead."

And again, next, he blames Eusebius for having preached in the church while passing through Ancyra at that time, things he says he learned by hearsay. Indignant at this, he writes as follows: "The Apostle writes such things about the faith of the Galatians. But Eusebius twisted the Apostle's meaning (for it was for the reason given above that the Apostle said, 'My children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you') and attacked the Galatians as though they did not hold a right opinion about God.

For he was truly suffering sharp and bitter labor pains, because he knew that the Galatians did not think as he did about piety, nor speak of two essences, two things, two powers and two gods." Notice how bitterly he reviles a man who, by his own account, said nothing more than the apostolic text. Here he admits that Eusebius speaks of two gods, inasmuch as Eusebius calls the Son of God God together with the Father. Yet further on, as if he had forgotten what he accused him of here, he tries to slander the same man as saying that Christ is a mere man.

Next, after what has been set out, he adds a great deal of long-winded drivel, stringing together for himself things that are so and things that are not, almost like those who said, "Our lips are our own; who is lord over us?"

This shows, as I said at the beginning of this work, that he leapt into writing out of excessive enmity and hatred of his brethren. Passing on from these things, he again makes a tragedy of Asterius, spinning out a long story about him too: how he travels, and where, and when, and to whom. Leaving this as well, he turns again to the man of God Paulinus, writing this in these very words:

"Persuaded by these words, Paulinus too, this man's father, does not hesitate to say and write the same things: at one time calling Christ a second god, who became god in a more human way, at another defining him as a creature. That this is so is shown by the fact that once, when he was passing through Ancyra, he told us too that Christ is a creature."

And again, telling tales, he says that he conversed with Paulinus. Then he slanders the blessed man as having spoken of many gods. Leaving Paulinus, he again busies himself with Eusebius, saying: "Eusebius of Caesarea also wrote in this way, since he too holds the same opinion about gods as Paulinus and the pagans.

For he wrote not as though God alone exists, but as though one of them is the only true God. It was from him, then, that Paulinus too, Asterius's father, learned to think that there are younger gods." Here too he blames them for introducing opinions about gods, while he himself denies the divinity of the Son. Having quoted Eusebius's words, he does not understand that the saying which teaches that the Father is the only true God was not Eusebius's

but our Savior's, who said, "that they may know you, the only true God." After other things he adds: "Otherwise, from what divine texts will they be able to show us that there is one unbegotten and one begotten in the way they believe he was begotten, when neither prophets nor evangelists nor apostles have said this?"

Then, as if he had signed up in the games to brawl with everyone at once, he passes on to Narcissus and says: "So that even if someone says that, establishing that there is a first god and a second, as Narcissus has written in these very words

(for the one who says, "Let us make man in our image and after our likeness," does not allow it), we have heard in part, from the Lord himself bearing witness and from the holy Scriptures, that he and his Father are two. If, then, Narcissus wishes on this account to divide the Word from the Father in power, let him know that the prophet who wrote that God had said, "Let us make man in our image and after our likeness," himself also wrote, "And God made man."

And passing from Narcissus to Asterius, he writes this: For Asterius declared that the Father and the Son are one and the same only in this respect, that they agree in all things. For this is what he said: "And because of their exact agreement in all words and deeds, 'I and the Father are one.'" And again he attacks Eusebius, saying: For they want the Savior to be a man. This is clear from the way Eusebius has craftily turned the words of the Apostle to suit his own purpose.
For as if wishing to bring forth the greatest blasphemy after some long-standing labor, "he poured out evil from his own treasure," as the Savior's saying puts it.

For, wishing to show that the Savior is only a man, as though he were uncovering for us a supremely secret mystery of the Apostle, he said this: "Therefore the divine Apostle too, handing down to us the secret and mystical theology, most plainly cries out and proclaims, 'There is one God,' and then, after the one God, he says, 'There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.'"

If, then, he says that he is a man, attending only to his dispensation in the flesh, he surely also concedes that one must not set one's hope on him. For the prophet Jeremiah said, "Cursed is the man who sets his hope on man."

You see how malice blinds. Earlier, at any rate, he himself testified that this man confesses the Son to be God, and even found fault with him for this, for presenting the Word of God as God subsisting in essence and power; now he slanders the same man as saying that Christ is a mere man, plainly lying both in what he has said and in what he goes on to add about him next, saying: "But the aforementioned, having paid scant attention to the holy prophets, and declaiming as though it were some secret and hidden theology of the Apostle, said, 'There is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.'"

And the man who wrote this, boasting so loudly of his knowledge of the Scriptures, did not notice that the most holy Apostle who wrote this also wrote that: "who, being in the form of God, did not regard being equal to God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of man, and being found in appearance as a man."

You see how the holy Apostle, as if foreseeing in the Spirit the mischief of these men, wrote in another passage "as a man" and "being made in the likeness of man," so as to put a stop to their great blasphemy. And after some further remarks he slanders the same man in roughly these words: How then can Eusebius, paying no attention to these things, want the Savior to be only a man?

Though he does not dare to say this openly, he wants it, and he is convicted by his own words. And yet the man who said this used to reproach the same Eusebius for proclaiming the Son to be God, writing as follows: For having dared to divide the Word of God, and having named the Word another God, separate from the Father in essence and in power, into how great a blasphemy has he fallen!

25. Since Marcellus has set out all this, and much more besides, not only against the bishops but also against the sound faith of the Church, it should be clear what sort of disposition he had. And that the man cared nothing for the truth you would learn by reading the bishops' letters themselves, in which you will find him mutilating the whole body of meaning of their words and concealing their entire train of thought, while seizing on scraps of phrases and maliciously making them the ground of his accusation.

Take for example how he openly slanders Eusebius as having said that Christ is a mere man, because in his own letter he quoted the words of the Apostle, in which the Apostle himself said, "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus."

So this apostolic saying he has attacked as if it were Eusebius's own, our most learned friend failing to realize that it was the Apostle he was attacking. But Eusebius's own words, those contained in the same letter and those in his other writings composed on the divine Scriptures, which have been circulated everywhere, he has passed over in silence, hiding by silence what could not be slandered.

One would find that he has done the same with the other writings he has attacked as well. These, out of regard for a proper length of discourse, we shall leave to those who wish to examine them closely, since we ourselves are eager now at last to expose Marcellus's own strange teaching about the Son of God, so that it may become plain to everyone what he himself thought about the Son of God.

Now that I have set out the men he slandered, the time has come to bring to light the Galatian's faith toward the Son of God, or rather his unbelief. I will get briefly past the façade of his letter and strip bare the false doctrine that has long lurked within the man. Using his own words as witnesses, I will show everyone what kind of man was presiding over the church of Christ. He held that the Son neither exists, nor pre-existed, nor ever existed at all for God before he was born through the virgin. He claimed that he is only a Word, connatural with God, eternally abiding with him and united to him, much like the word that is in a human being.

For he himself uses this very comparison. He says that there is a Word within God himself, sometimes at rest and sometimes active in expressing meaning, and that it proceeds from the Father by activity alone, just as we too are active in speaking and talking when we give some command. But it is obvious to anyone that no one would call a word that expresses meaning and acts in this way a Son. Yet after granting this of God, he somehow claims that this Word, which has no real existence of its own, took on the flesh and acted in it,

and that only then did it become Christ, Jesus, King, Image of God, Beloved, glorified Son, and even Firstborn of all creation. Though it did not exist before, it became these things then, even without having a real existence of its own. And the most astonishing part of his account is this: all these things began not even a full four hundred years ago, and all of them will cease at once after the time of judgment. Then the Word will be united to God, so that there is nothing else but God, and the flesh it took on will be left abandoned by the Word. So at that time neither the Son of God will exist, nor the Son of Man whom he took on.

This is the end he arrives at, as though he were deaf. He does not hear the angel Gabriel, who announced the good news to the Mother of God clearly and explicitly about the one who would be born of her and would come forth "from the seed of David according to the flesh." Gabriel said: "Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." Nor does he understand the words of Daniel, the great prophet, who sealed these very things in what he foretold in the divine Spirit, saying: "And behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he reached the Ancient of Days and was brought before him.

And to him were given dominion and honor and kingdom, and all peoples, tribes and tongues will serve him. His authority is an everlasting authority that will not pass away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed." Nor was he persuaded by Isaiah, who himself prophesied as follows about the unending kingdom of the Son of Man: "For a child has been born to us, a son has also been given to us,

whose dominion is upon his shoulder, and his name is called Messenger of Great Counsel, Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Ruler, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come. For I will bring peace and health to him.
Great is his dominion, and of his peace there will be no end, upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and uphold it with justice and with righteousness, from now and forever."

What Gabriel announced to the virgin agreed with these words, for he said that the one born of her would reign "forever" and that "of his kingdom" there would be no end. But you can learn from Marcellus's own words how he dared to write the opposite of all this. In them he denied both the divinity and the humanity of the Son of God, in a way more novel than any godless heresy.

Among the heterodox, some said that the Son of God was not pre-existent and did not exist beforehand. They supposed him to be a man like everyone else, born of a man, and said that he had been honored with adoption as son. But having granted this, they confessed that he has deathless and unending honor and glory and an eternal kingdom. Others denied that the man was the Son of God and posited a pre-existent God. These men, strangers to the church, went only so far in their error. But the man who presided for so long over the church of God abolishes the very existence of the Son of God. He served at the Son's altar, and perhaps believes that he himself will attain eternal and immortal life, while he deprives its High Priest of that life.

Yet, as the apostle says, we have "a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God." Marcellus dares to say that he neither existed before nor pre-existed. Worse, he says that he will not exist hereafter, nor be with the saints of God when that promise of the kingdom of heaven is fulfilled. For at that time, when all the saints will share in the kingdom of God in incorruptible and immortal bodies, he deprives Christ alone, and the flesh he took on, of it.

He does not shudder to declare that the author of the resurrection, the cause of eternal life for all, will lose not only the kingdom but life itself. It is as if someone were to grant the eyes but abolish the light that supplies their brightness. Neither Gabriel, so great an angel of God, nor the great prophet Daniel, of whom it was said, "Are you wiser than Daniel?", nor Isaiah, great as he was, nor the rest of the chorus of prophets persuaded the man not to write or think such things.

Nor did the Jews themselves, among whom the Christ is still awaited today. They usually call him "the Anointed," and they hope that he will have an ageless and deathless kingdom. But Marcellus has become worse even than they are, for he has dared to commit impiety against both the beginning and the end of the Son of God. Not even the divine apostle could shame him out of such impiety, though he says plainly: "The saying is trustworthy: if we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him." The apostle also says that we shall be heirs of God, but not apart from Christ, for he says: "heirs

of God and joint heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him." And again he says: "But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him, knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, will never die again; death will no longer have dominion over him."

And again: "But the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." So eternal life will be provided to us in no other way than "in Christ Jesus our Lord." Our hope is not simply to live, but to be glorified with him, to inherit with him, and to reign with him, for everything will be ours through our fellowship with him.

The same apostle teaches this when he says: "God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord." And he shows what this fellowship is when he says: "And he raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, so that in the ages to come he might show the surpassing riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus."

The same apostle also taught these things about the Savior: "But he, because he remains forever, holds his priesthood permanently. Therefore he is able to save completely those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them."

Moreover, he said that Melchizedek too remains a priest "forever" because he has been made like "the Son of God." A little later I will set out how Marcellus dared to write the opposite of all these things. But first let us look at what he thought when he held that the Son of God does not exist at all and has no real existence.

After censuring those who have said that the Son of God is truly a Son, living and subsisting, he makes his own opinion plain, writing in these very words: "So before he came down and was born through the Virgin, he was only Word. For what else was it, before it took up human flesh, that came down 'in the last days', as he too has written, and that was born of the Virgin? It was nothing other than Word."

Then, going on, he calls him eternal, and in this way defines him as unbegotten. He writes as follows: "Do you hear, then, the harmony of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness through many different persons to the eternity of the Word?

And for this reason he begins from the eternity of the Word, saying: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.' By using three successive testimonies he means to show the eternity of the Word." And after other things he adds: "For before, as I have often said, he was nothing other than Word."

And he adds that he was not even "the image of the invisible God," saying: "So it is perfectly clear that before he took up our body the Word in himself was not the image of the invisible God." And again, after other things, he goes on: "What then was this that came down before he became man? Surely, he will say, spirit. For if he should wish to say anything other than this, the angel who said to the Virgin, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you,' will not allow him. But if he says it is spirit, hear the Saviour saying, 'God is spirit.'"

Since the Saviour clearly said this of the Father, "God is spirit," Marcellus stands convicted from these words of saying that the Father himself became man. Yet he strives still further, writing as follows: "Let him learn, then, that the Word of God has come—not a Word so named by a loose use of the term, as they say, but one who is truly Word."

And again he adds this to what has been said: "For if the Spirit alone were examined, he would rightly appear to be one and the same with God; but if the addition according to the flesh is examined in the case of the Saviour, the Godhead seems to be extended by activity alone. So it is rightly, in truth, an indivisible Monad."

And he establishes this still further by what he writes next: "To say, then, that he was begotten before the ages he seems to have said consistently, for what has proceeded from the Father who sent it forth becomes his offspring. But the other point he has not taken up soundly or piously.

For to say that the one who proceeded from him is not Word, and that this is not the true manner of the generation, but simply that he is only Son, tends to give those who hear it the impression of some human figure." In these words he has barefacedly denied the Son; and that he introduces a mere word, like some command about things to be done, is clear from what he goes on to say: "whom all the divine Scriptures thus proclaim.

For David says of him, 'By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm.' And again the same writer: 'He sent out his word and healed them.' And Solomon: 'The wicked will seek me and will not find me, for they hated wisdom and did not choose the word of the Lord.' And Isaiah said: 'For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.'

And again Jeremiah says: 'The wise were put to shame, and terrified, and caught, because they rejected the word of the Lord.' And Hosea the prophet said: 'They hated the one who reproves in the gates, and they abhorred the holy word.' And Micah likewise, he too making mention of the word, said: 'Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.'"

Collecting so many passages about the commanding word, Marcellus says that the God the Word who was "in the beginning with God" is also something of this kind. So he goes on to say: "But the holy apostle and disciple of the Lord, John, teaching clearly and expressly at the beginning of the Gospel, as about something previously unknown among men, and naming him Word of the Almighty, spoke thus: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.' Using not just one testimony, he signifies the eternity of the Word.

And he adds to this, saying next: "so that by saying 'In the beginning was the Word' he might show that the Word is in the Father in potency (for God is the beginning of all things that have come into being, 'from whom are all things'); and by 'and the Word was with God,' that the Word is with God in activity (for 'all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being');

and by saying that the Word is God, that he might not divide the Godhead, since the Word is in him and he in the Word. For he says, 'The Father is in me, and I in the Father.'" And to this he adds still more, laying bare his own mind in what he brings in next, saying: "So the holy apostle and disciple of the Lord, John, in recalling his eternity, became a true witness of the Word, saying, 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.'

Making no mention here of any generation of the Word, but using three successive testimonies, he confirmed that the Word was in the beginning." And he adds to this, saying: "The economy according to the flesh we know to belong to the man; but the eternity according to the spirit we have believed to be united to the Father."

Going on further, he next says this: "If then he himself says, 'I came forth from the Father and have come,' and again, 'And the word that you hear is not mine, but the Father's who sent me,' and 'All that the Father has is mine,' it is clear that he fittingly said this too: 'The Father is in me, and I in the Father,' so that the Word who says this is in God, and the Father is in the Word, because the Word is the power of the Father.

For a trustworthy witness has called him 'the power of God and the wisdom of God.' So it is not because of exact agreement in all words and deeds, as Asterius said, that the Saviour says, 'I and the Father are one,' but because it is impossible for either the Word to be divided from God or God from his own Word.
