For if Asterius thinks that the Saviour said this because of agreement in all things, and is unwilling to learn the truth by attending to the second economy, it is necessary to remind him how at times one can see what [?] appears to be disagreement.

For this is what the passages teach us. What agreement was there, at the time of the passion, when he says, 'Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass,' and then adds, 'Yet not as I will, but as you will'? For first, to say 'Let this cup pass' was not the speech of one in agreement; and what follows also seems to have nothing to do with agreement, for he says, 'Not my will but yours be done, Father.'

You hear how the letter shows apparent disagreement, one willing and the other not willing. That the Father willed is clear from the fact that what he willed came to pass; that the Son did not will is clear from his begging to be spared. And again he says, 'I do not seek my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me.'

How then does he say that the Saviour said 'I and the Father are one' because of agreement in all things?" And after a little he adds: "How can the Son be in agreement with the Father, or the Father with the Son, when the Son says, 'All that the Father has is mine'? For to say 'All that the Father has is mine' was plainly the speech of a Son claiming more than the Father.

For this is why, passing over the phrase 'All that the Father has is common,' he said, 'All that the Father has is mine.' And yet it was not characteristic of one in agreement to speak like this, but rather: All that the Father has is common. For if the Acts of the Apostles, praising the concord of those who were then coming to the faith, said, 'They had all things in common,' and if one ought to consider that even among human beings who are able to agree all things are common, how much more ought the Father and the Son to have shared in fellowship, divided as they are into two hypostases? But as it is, in saying 'All that the Father has is mine,' the Son appears to claim more than the Father; while in declaring that he is not master even of his own word, but that the Father is master of this too

('for the word that you hear,' he says, 'is not mine, but the Father's who sent me'), he shows the Father taking away what belongs to the Child. Yet on Asterius's supposition both statements appear to have been said inconsistently.

For one who is in agreement ought not to snatch away the rights belonging to the other—that is greedy—but to regard what belongs to each as common. So when we look to the human flesh, we shall not find that the Saviour said 'I and the Father are one' in the sense Asterius has written; for it was not because of exact agreement in all words and deeds, as he has written, that the Saviour said, 'I and the Father are one.'

For if that were so, he would surely have said: I and the Father agree with one another in all things. But as it is, he said, 'I and the Father are one.' So if there was some disagreement in those matters, and the Master must speak the truth, it is fitting to know precisely concerning the Saviour that whenever he says 'I and the Father are one,' he says this not with a view to the man whom he assumed, but to the Word who came forth from the Father.

For if there should seem to be some disagreement, it ought to be referred to the weakness of the flesh, which the Word assumed without having had it before. But if oneness is spoken of, it plainly belongs to the Word.

That is why he fittingly said not only 'I and the Father are one,' but also, 'Have I been with you so long, Philip, and you say, Show me the Father?'—clearly not with these eyes, but with the eyes of the mind, which are able to see intelligible things. For both the Father and his Word are invisible to the eyes of the flesh. So it was not because of agreement in all things that he said this to Philip."

Having said so much, he takes up his argument again from the beginning and lays down his doctrine in this way: "For before all creation there was a certain stillness, as was natural, since the Word was in God. For if Asterius has believed God to be the maker of all things, it is clear that he too will agree with us that God always exists, never having taken a beginning of being, while the other things came into being by him and came into being out of nothing. For I do not suppose that in this matter too he believes the one who says that there are also some unbegotten things, but rather that he is firmly persuaded that heaven and earth and all things in the heavens and on the earth have come into being by God.
If, then, he believes this, he must also agree that besides God there was nothing else. The Word, then, had his own glory, being in the Father."

And having said this, he goes on after other things: "Asterius calls the authority given to him glory—and not merely glory, but glory before the world—not realizing that when the world had not yet come into being there was nothing else besides God alone."

Having said this, and having thereby openly denied the Son, Marcellus, in order to persuade us precisely what sort of thing he thought the Word of God to be, displays his meaning still more clearly by likening him to our own word, writing as follows: "For just as all things that have come into being by the Father have come into being through the Word, so too the things spoken by the Father are signified through the Word. This is why the most holy Moses here calls the Word an angel: because he appeared for no other reason than to announce to Moses what he knew would benefit the sons of Israel; and he knew that it would benefit them to hold that God is one.

That is why he said to him, 'I am he who is,' so as to teach that there is no other god besides himself. And this, I think, is easy for the right-minded to understand even from a small and lowly example taken from ourselves.

For no one can separate a man's word from him in power and in hypostasis; for the word is one and the same with the man, and is separated from him by nothing else than the activity of action alone." And he is still more lavish in displaying his meaning in what he says next: "For God did not need any other preparation for the construction, such as matter or any other human kind, but only this preparation in his own mind.

Since, then, it was impossible for God to think about the construction of the heaven without Word and the wisdom belonging to the Word, he fittingly said, 'When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him.'" And again he adds, likening the Word of God to the human word so as to show that he has no subsistence; he writes as follows: "Here the Father says to Moses, 'I am he who is'; but he says it, clearly, through the Word.

For whatever the Father says, he is everywhere seen to say through the Word. And this is clear from ourselves as well, so far as small things may be likened to great and divine ones; for we too do everything that we wish to say and do, as far as we are able, by our own word."

Then, after saying some things in between, he adds: "How then did Asterius, who pretends to follow the holy Scriptures simply and with reverent fear, fail to recognize this passage, which says, 'The Lord your God, he is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath, and there is none other besides him,' and that 'he is one,' and besides him 'there is no' other?"

And going on he again insists, saying: "not named Word by a loose use of the term—even if those who teach otherwise burst with their lies—but being Word properly and truly." And he adds: "For what other mystery was hidden but the one concerning the Word? This mystery was formerly so hidden 'in God' that none of the former people clearly knew the things concerning the Word, whereas we now enjoy the riches 'of the glory' and of the hidden mystery."

And after this he again makes use of a human image, writing in this way: "For who, whether of the holy angels or of righteous men, was so worthy of trust as to undo the punishment decreed against him by the very face of God,

except the Word himself, who was present with him and joined in fashioning him, to whom the Father said, 'Let us make man after our image and likeness'—since there was no other god able to join him in fashioning? For 'I am,' he says, 'the first God, and I am after these things, and besides me there is no other God.' So there was neither some younger god, nor was anyone else, being a god 'after these things,' able to work together with God.

But suppose someone, using a small human example from our own experience, should examine the divine action as through an image. A skilled sculptor, wishing to mould a statue, first considers its forms and features within himself; then he thinks out what breadth and height would be fitting, and examines the proportion of the whole in each individual part. Having prepared the suitable material of bronze, and having sketched out beforehand in his own mind the statue that is to be, and thinking that he sees it with his mind, and being aware that his word—by which he reasons and by which he is accustomed to do everything (for nothing that does not come about by reason is beautiful)—is working together with him, he begins this work perceptible to the senses and exhorts himself as though another, saying: Come, let us make, come, let us mould a statue. In the same way the God and Master of all, when making the living statue from the earth, exhorts no one else but his own Word, saying, 'Let us make man'—not in the same way as the other things, for the whole creation came into being by a word."

And after other things he adds to this: "But as it is, I believe the divine Scriptures, that there is one God, and that his Word, as God, came forth from the Father, so that 'all things' might come into being 'through him.' But after the time of judgment and the setting right of all things and the abolishing of all opposing activity, 'then he himself will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him,' 'to God and the Father,' so that the Word may thus be in God, just as he was before the world existed. For since nothing existed before except God alone, and all things were going to come into being through the Word, the Word came forth by effective activity, this Word being the Father's."

And again he puts the same thought more plainly, saying: "For before the world existed, the Word was in the Father. But when God Almighty purposed to make all things in the heavens and on the earth, the coming into being of the world required effective activity. And for this reason, since nothing else existed besides God (for all things are acknowledged to have come into being by him), the Word then came forth and became the maker of the world—he who before had also been preparing it inwardly in thought."

And again, after all this, he goes on to say: "And for this reason he does not call himself Son of God, but everywhere calls himself Son of Man, so that by such a confession he might bring it about that man, through fellowship with him, becomes son of God by adoption, and that after the completion of the work he might again, as Word, be united to God, fulfilling what was foretold by the apostle: 'Then he himself will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all and in all.' For then he will be what he was before." With so many words Marcellus barefacedly forswore the Son of God.

For if God and the Word in him were one and the same, and no one could ever become his own father, just as no one could be his own son, being one and alone; and if God was one alone and the same as his own Word, it is clear that he was not a Father, since he had no Son, nor was the Word a Son, since no Father subsisted for him.

What sort of things the man set forth, then, about the Son of God neither existing nor having existed beforehand, but being a mere word dwelling within God himself, at one time at rest and at another active with effective power, we have learned from the passages quoted above. By setting out these same things many times and in various ways in his writing, he has heaped up a great pile of superfluous words in his treatise. But we, content with the refutations of himself that come from the very words he set out, shall not even deem the absurdity of this Jewish doctrine worthy of a rebuttal.

From here, let us pass on to what the same man has said about the flesh, which he says the Word in God assumed by activity alone, and let us see how he transfers to the flesh the theology concerning the only-begotten Son of God that is found in the divine Scriptures—denying the true Son of God himself, who truly existed beforehand, while proclaiming the divinity of the flesh, which this irreverent man declared would shortly afterwards be left bereft of the Word.

"For the Word 'was in the beginning,' being nothing other than Word. But the man united to the Word, who did not exist before, became man, as John teaches us when he says, 'And the Word became flesh.' For this reason, then, he appears to mention the Word alone; for whenever the divine Scripture mentions the name of Jesus or of Christ, it appears to be naming the Word of God as existing together with the human flesh. And if anyone should claim to be able to show the name of Christ or of Jesus applied to the Word alone even before the New Testament, he will find that it was spoken prophetically, as is clear from this passage too: 'The kings of the earth stood up,' it says, 'and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.'"

And after other things he adds: "Fittingly, then, before the descent he was what we have often said, Word; but after the descent and the assumption of the flesh he also received various titles, since 'the Word became flesh.'" Observe how by these words Marcellus does not want the names Jesus and Christ and the other titles to apply to the Word, but to the flesh which he assumed. This observation is necessary, so that when he in turn casts off the flesh, he may be convicted of impiety against the very Christ of God. After what has been quoted, he proceeds in order and writes the following about the body of the Saviour:

"And let Asterius not think it implausible that his body, though younger, was able to attain such great antiquity. Let him rather consider that, even if the human flesh is indeed younger, nevertheless the Word, who deigned to assume it through a pure virgin and united himself to it, not only made the man created in himself 'the firstborn of all creation,' but also wills him to be the beginning of all things, not only of things on earth but also of things in heaven."

Having said this much, and then other things, he refers to the flesh those words of the apostle in which he speaks of the Son of God as God, saying: 'He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; for in him all things were created, in the heavens and on earth, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities; all things were created through him and for him; and he is before all things, and in him all things hold together.' He does not blush to take such words of the apostle as referring to the flesh. Yet as he goes on, Marcellus himself writes this about that same flesh: "If, then, (the Saviour) confesses that the flesh profits nothing, how is it possible for what is from the earth and profits nothing to be with the Word in the ages to come, as though it were of benefit to him?"

And again about the same flesh he adds: "How could the form of the servant, which the Word assumed, being the form of a servant, still possibly [?] be with the Word?" Yet the man who said such things about the flesh now calls it 'the image of God' and 'the firstborn of all creation,' and says that it exists before all things, 'and that all things in the heavens and on earth, thrones, dominions, rulers, authorities, were created in it.'

He writes as follows: "Therefore, if he is 'the firstborn of all creation,' and 'in him all things were created,' we ought to know that the apostle is here speaking of his economy according to the flesh." And he confirms the statement by adding next: "He was therefore named 'the firstborn of all creation' because of his birth according to the flesh, not because of the first creation, as they suppose."

And he adds: "This most holy Word, then, was not named 'the firstborn of all creation' before the incarnation (for how is it possible for one who always exists to be the firstborn of anything?). Rather, it is the first 'new man,' in whom God willed 'to sum up all things,' whom the divine Scriptures name 'the firstborn of all creation.'" And again he adds: "You hear how not only these things but also the things that existed before, 'in the heavens and on earth,' turn out to have been 'created in him' in accordance with the new creation."

These, then, are the words in which he has said that he was named firstborn of all creation because of the flesh. But see how he again refers to the flesh the words 'The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works,' paying no heed to the divine Scripture, which speaks in the person of Wisdom in Proverbs in this way: 'I, Wisdom, have made counsel my dwelling, and I have called upon knowledge and understanding; through me kings reign, and princes decree justice.'

To these words the same Wisdom next adds: 'I walk in the ways of righteousness, and I go about in the midst of the paths of justice, so that I may give substance to those who love me and fill their treasuries with good things. If I declare to you the things that happen day by day, I will remember to recount the things from of old.'

'The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works; before the age he founded me; in the beginning, before he made the earth,' and what follows. Marcellus refused to give these words his attention. Having only one aim, not to confess the Son of God, he refers the theology before us to the flesh, and, turning aside from the straight road, he has devised for himself a path where there is none, writing word for word as follows:

"This chapter of Proverbs, then, said 'The Lord created me' with no wish to present the beginning of our Saviour's divinity, as they think, but rather his second economy, according to the flesh. That is why it fittingly speaks of creation, the creation of the human flesh."

And next he adds: "So the creation concerns his work as man. That is why it says, 'The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works': that is, he created me through the Virgin Mary, through whom God chose to unite the human flesh to his own Word."

And after other things he goes on to say: "This being so, it follows that we should consider in our minds this chapter, spoken in proverbial fashion: 'The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works.' For our Master, God, truly created, since he made what did not exist; the flesh which the Word assumed did not exist, and he created it when it did not exist." And again he adds: "So this is the meaning of 'The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works.'"

He continues: "'Before the age he founded me': he calls this foundation the economy according to the flesh that was foreordained for him. As the apostle also says, 'For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.' And here he mentions one age, from which he said the things concerning Christ had been founded."

And again he confirms the same phrase, saying: "Fittingly the prophet said, 'Before the age he founded me,' meaning, that is, what is according to the flesh, because of its fellowship with the Word, his true Son." And next he adds: "Then he says, 'In the beginning, before he made the earth.' What earth is this, if not clearly our flesh, which after the disobedience became earth again? For 'you are earth,' he says, 'and to earth you shall return.' This flesh had to obtain healing by sharing in some way in the holy Word."

But see how Marcellus contradicts himself here. Having said elsewhere that ⟨the flesh⟩ was 'the beginning of the ways' of God which was created, and having said again that this same flesh was the 'foundation,' he goes on to 'before he made the earth.' Then he interprets the earth as the flesh once more, failing to see how incoherent it is to say that the flesh was created before the flesh, and then, after the creation of the flesh, to speak of the flesh again.

But beyond this he goes on next to say: "Then he says, 'before he made the depths.' Here the prophet, speaking in proverbs, says that the depths are the hearts of the saints, which hold the gift of the Spirit in their own depths."

Note in this too how, having taken 'The Lord created me' as spoken of the flesh, and then finding himself hard pressed by the Scripture that says 'before he made the depths,' he interprets the depths as the hearts of the saints. Yet he fails to see that the hearts of the saints, that is, of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, of Moses, Elijah and Melchizedek, and of the rest of the prophets, came into being before the Saviour's flesh.

How then is it possible to refer 'before he made the depths' to the flesh? And after other things he again goes on to say: "What, then, is ⟨this⟩ chapter, 'before the springs ⟨of the waters came forth'? He says they are the holy apostles.⟩ The book of Exodus presents this mystery to us, foretelling long ago the types of the apostles; for since the apostles are twelve in number, it mentions twelve springs."

And again he adds the same thing, writing as follows: "Fittingly, then, the Master, speaking through the prophet Solomon about his birth according to the flesh, said, 'before the springs of the waters came forth.'"

Then, after going through some other matters, he adds: "Since, then, we have spoken of what comes first, it follows that we should also fill in what remains. What remains is the passage about the mountains and the hills. For 'before the mountains were settled,' it says, 'and before all the hills, he begets me.' By mountains and hills he means the apostles and the apostles' successors, so as to signify, in proverbial fashion, how their righteous way of life stands out above that of other people."

Having set out interpretations of this kind, he passes again to the apostle's words, saying the very opposite of what the apostle said. For the apostle taught that the preexistent Son of God is also 'the firstborn of all creation,' that 'all things' were created 'through him and in him,' and that he is 'before all things,' testifying to this with a loud cry. Marcellus, however, drags this theology too down to the flesh, and a little later he denies even this.

He speaks as follows: "For this reason he fittingly adds, 'who is the image of the invisible God.' When did he become an image? Was it not when he assumed the creature formed 'after the image and likeness'? For before that, as I have often said, he was nothing other than Word." And he persists, explaining the same point more baldly, in these words: "It is therefore obvious that before he assumed our body, the Word in himself was not the image of the invisible God. For an image must be seen, so that through the image what was until then unseen may be seen."

And again he adds: "How, then, has Asterius written that the Word of God is the image of the invisible God? For images show the things whose images they are even when those things are absent, so that the absent one seems to appear through them. But if, since God is invisible, the Word is also invisible, how can the Word in himself be the image of the invisible God, when he too is invisible? For it is impossible for what is not visible ever to be made manifest through what is invisible."

In this too Marcellus fails to see that if we grant that the flesh is the image of God, it is time to say that the flesh of all people and the faces of their bodies are images of God, so that, on his view, the Saviour had nothing exceptional about him. But as though he had forgotten what he later wrote about the flesh (calling it 'the form of a servant' on the strength of the apostle's words, and saying that for this reason it cannot be with the Word, because it is 'the form of a servant,'

and even saying openly, "How is it possible for what is from the earth and profits nothing to be with the Word in the ages to come?"), he insists that at present the flesh is the image of the invisible God, declaring outright that before he assumed our body, God's Word was not the image of the invisible God.

20 And again, after the passages already quoted, he adds: "Therefore it is clear from every side that the holy apostle called the flesh that was joined to the Word the image of the invisible God, so that through what is visible the invisible too might appear. 'He is,' says the apostle, 'the image of the invisible God.' Now, that is, when he assumed the flesh made after the image of God, he became the true image of the invisible God."

"For if through this image we have been counted worthy to know the Word of God, we ought to believe the Word himself when he says through the image, 'I and the Father are one.' For no one can know either the Word or the Father of the Word apart from this image."

And again he adds: "So too the apostle says, as we said a little earlier, 'He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,' signifying to us by the form of the servant the human flesh. As our Master, God, was fashioning this flesh by his own Wisdom, he said of it, 'Let us make man after our image and likeness,' rightly calling the human flesh an image. For he knew precisely that a little later it would be the image of his own Word."

After this he tries to establish that 'From the womb before the morning star I begot you' was also said of the flesh, and he writes as follows: "For this reason, then, since the prophet David fittingly gave the name morning star to the star that announces the day, it is no longer right to ask who this morning star might be. For it was the star that appeared at that time, bringing and announcing the day to the magi."

"It is obvious, then, that 'Before the morning star I begot you' was spoken by the almighty Master about the Word born through the Virgin together with the human flesh. The Gospel also indicates this clearly: first our Master was born through the Virgin, and afterwards the star appeared that showed forth the day."

Proceeding further, he adds: "For the man received authority not only over affairs on earth but also over those in heaven, and fittingly so. For if, when he became both 'man' and 'mediator between God and men,' 'all things were then created for him,' as the apostle said, 'both those in heaven and those on earth,' it follows that we should know precisely that authority has been given him not only over things on earth but also over things in heaven." And again, after other things, he continues: "For if the holy Gospel speaks of some glory given to him by the Father, it is evident that the man received this glory through the Word. For having become, as the holy apostle says, 'mediator between God and men,' he glorified godly people with the glory given to him by the Father."

And again he adds this: "And he deemed the man who had fallen through disobedience worthy to be joined through the Virgin to his own Word. For what greater glory could there be among men than this? And having said, 'I have glorified you,' he adds, 'and I will glorify again.' He says this so that, through his surpassing love for humanity, in the second glory after the resurrection of the flesh he might make the formerly mortal man immortal, and glorify him with such glory that he would not only be freed from his former slavery but would also be counted worthy of a glory beyond what is human."

And again he adds: "so that, as I said, he might enable the man who had formerly been deceived by the devil to conquer the devil in his turn. That is why he assumed the man: so that he might duly enable him to receive the firstfruits of authority." And he goes on further to say: "For this is the beloved, the man united to the Word, of whom the evangelist said, 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.'"

And again he adds: "that the Word of the invisible God was to be born through a virgin and to assume human flesh, so that through it he might overcome the devil who had formerly prevailed over man, and make man not only incorruptible and immortal but also enthroned with God in heaven."

All this must be kept in mind because of what Marcellus himself is going to bring forward against the flesh which the Word of God assumed. For as though he had forgotten everything he set out here, he brings upon the Saviour's body an end that is neither auspicious nor pious. On top of all this, as though his earlier arguments had succeeded, he tries to show that 'The Lord has reigned; let the earth rejoice' also refers to the flesh.

He speaks as follows: "He, then, who came down and took on flesh through the Virgin was appointed king over the church, evidently so that through the Word the man who had formerly fallen from the kingdom of heaven might be able to attain a kingdom. It was because God wished this man, who had formerly fallen from the kingdom through disobedience, to become Lord and God that he carried out this economy. So the most holy prophet David says prophetically, 'The Lord has reigned; let the earth rejoice.'"

And after other things he adds: "For this reason the prophecy says, 'But I have been appointed king by him,' as though our Master Christ had received the beginning of his kingship from some point in time." And again he adds: "For this is why he will reign: so that the man who was formerly deceived, having come to be in human flesh and having been appointed king through the Word, 'will abolish every rule' of the devil, 'and every power and authority.'"

He has said this much about the Saviour's flesh, and a great deal more besides. He has declared that it is the image 'of the invisible God,' the firstborn 'of all creation,' the king, Jesus, Christ, the beloved, and whatever else he listed, and has stated that it is on account of the flesh that the Word was called all these things. Now it is time to see what kind of end he assigns to it.

"For this is why he will reign, having come to be in human flesh; and the man who was formerly deceived, once he has been made king through the Word, 'will abolish every rule' of the devil 'and every power and authority.' 'For he must reign,' it says, 'until he has put his enemies under his feet.' So the holy apostle says that this is the end of the kingdom of our Lord Christ: that all things be subjected under his feet." And a little later he adds: "Here the apostle reveals to us a very great mystery, saying that there will be an end of Christ's kingdom, and that the end will come when all things have been subjected under his feet."

And working out the same argument still further, he writes as follows: "We said in our earlier statements that our Lord Christ had a beginning of his kingdom, and we used proofs from the divine Scriptures. One passage says, 'But I was established as king by him on Zion, his holy mountain';

another, 'The Lord has become king; let the peoples rage'; and again, 'The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice.' In short, one could easily produce countless passages as testimony to show that the man received a beginning of kingship through the Word. If, then, he received a beginning of kingship no more than four hundred years ago in all, it is nothing strange that the apostle says that he who obtained this kingdom so short a time ago will hand the kingdom over, clearly to God, who, as Scripture says, established him as king."

And after other things he writes as follows: "So he appears to have been separated from the Father by activity alone, because of the flesh, until the coming time of judgment appears, so that, once those who pierced him have seen the one they pierced, as the prophecy says, what remains may then follow in due order.

For since at the time of the end all things are to be subjected to Christ, as the apostle said, then 'he himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him.' What, then, are we taught about the human flesh which the Word assumed for our sake not quite four hundred years ago? Will the Word have it in the ages to come as well, or only until the time of judgment? For what the prophet said must be confirmed in deed: 'They shall look,' he says, 'on him whom they pierced'; and what they pierced was clearly the flesh."

And after other things he adds: "For the Word assumed our flesh not so that the Word might gain any benefit, but so that the flesh might obtain immortality through its fellowship with the Word. This is clear from the Savior's own declaration. For about the flesh he had while he conversed with the disciples, he says: 'Does this offend you? What then if you see the Son of Man going away to where he was before? It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh is of no benefit.' If, then, he acknowledges that the flesh is of no benefit to him, how can something that is from the earth and of no benefit remain united with the Word in the ages to come as well, as though it were of advantage to him?

This, it seems to me, is why the almighty Lord also says to him, 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.' He seems to separate him by activity alone because of the human flesh, and, as if fixing for him a definite time for sitting at the right hand, he says to him, 'until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.'

The holy apostle, interpreting this prophetic saying of David more clearly for us, put it something like this: 'For he must reign until he has made his enemies a footstool for his feet.' So his dispensation and kingdom as man appears to have a definite limit. For the apostle's words, 'until he has made his enemies a footstool for his feet,' mean nothing other than this.

So when he has his enemies as a footstool for his feet, he no longer needs this partial kingdom, since he is king of all things universally; for he reigns together with 'God and Father,' whose Word he both was and is.

For it was not the Word himself, in his own right, who received a beginning of kingship. Rather, the man who had been deceived by the devil became king through the power of the Word, so that, having become king, he might conquer the devil who had once deceived him. This is why the Acts of the Apostles also teach about this man, whom the Word of God assumed and with whom, having assumed him, he sits at the right hand of the Father, saying: 'whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration.' They too speak this way as if marking out a limit and an appointed term, within which the dispensation as man is fittingly united to the Word.

For what else does 'until the times of restoration' mean, if not to point us to a coming age in which all things must attain perfect restoration? If, then, Paul said that at the time of the restoration of all things even creation itself will be changed from slavery into freedom (for he says 'that creation itself will be set free from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God'),

how could the form of a slave, which the Word assumed and which is the form of a slave, still remain united with the Word? Clearly and expressly, then, the Word's dispensation in the flesh has taken place for our sake within a brief span of time set between the ages past and the ages to come. And the divine Paul said that, just as it had a beginning, so it will have an end, putting it like this: 'Then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God and Father.'"

After other things he goes on: "So it was not for his own sake but for ours that he assumed the human flesh. And if he evidently assumed it for our sake, and everything concerning us will be brought to its end by his providence and activity at the time of judgment, then there will no longer be any need even of this partial kingdom." Having said this, Marcellus then realized that he had fallen into absurdity, and added to what he had said: "But if someone should say that the human flesh is worthy of the Word because he made it immortal through the resurrection, let him know that not everything immortal is worthy of God.

For God is greater even than immortality itself, since by his own will he can make immortal even things that are not immortal. And that not everything immortal is worthy of being united to God is clear also from the fact that principalities, authorities and angels, though they are immortal, have no part in the unity of God."

Having said this, and realizing that he had fallen, as it were, into an abyss of absurdity, he tries to pull himself back, in a way confessing that he understood nothing of what he was saying. So he goes on: "But if someone should ask about this flesh which has become immortal in the Word, what do we say to him? That we do not think it safe to lay down doctrine about things we have not learned precisely from the divine Scriptures.
For how could those who also overturn the doctrines of others do such a thing?

But to those who wish to learn from us the precise account of this matter, we will say that, in obedience to the holy apostle, we know that we must see the hidden mysteries in the way he himself said: 'For now we see through a mirror, in a riddle, but then face to face; now we know in part, but then we shall know fully, even as we have been fully known.' So do not question me about things I have not clearly learned from divine Scripture.

For this reason, then, I will not be able to speak clearly about that divine flesh which shared in the divine Word either. But for now I believe the divine Scriptures, that God is one, and that his Word came forth from the Father so that 'all things' might come into being 'through him'; and that after the time of judgment, the setting right of all things, and the destruction of every opposing power, 'then he himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him,' 'to God and Father,' so that the Word may thus be in God, just as he was before."
Such is the end this admirable writer has assigned to the flesh of our Savior, forgetting what he had said about it earlier.

Then, after declaring so clearly that the Savior's body will be left bereft of the Word after the time of judgment, he puts on a show of reverence and says he does not know how to answer if someone should ask him about the flesh, and that he would say to the questioner: "Do not question me about things I have not learned."

But anyone at all might have said to him: Why then do you make a fool of yourself, man? Why do you push yourself over cliffs, laying down definitions in writing about things you have not learned? Why do you not keep what you received from the church's fathers and teachers? Instead you openly innovate, bringing into the world a new and strange perversion: you give the kingdom of Christ a temporary and recent beginning and posit an end for it, you deny the truly only-begotten Son of God, and you suppose a mere Word, without substance and without subsistence, which you say is nothing other than one and the same with God. Anyone who denies the Son of God might well say exactly that.

For a Word that does not subsist is not a Son, just as the word in a man could never be called the man's son, since it exists only as an activity in the one who speaks. Yet you say over and over that this Word became Son of God from the Father not quite four hundred years ago, through the assumption of the flesh; that he was then named Jesus and Christ, and was called image 'of the invisible God' and 'firstborn of all creation,' and indeed that he then became king. He began all these things, you say, from the time mentioned, and at the time of the consummation he will cease from all of them at once.

Where, then, did you learn these things? Who was your teacher in them? Which of the bishops, what synods, what writing of churchmen? And where, on your view, would the Savior's immortal body go? For since you confess it to be immortal and call it divine, you will surely suppose it to be incorruptible and indissoluble as well. And being of such a nature, it plainly remains intact and undissolved. But you took the Word away from it and joined him to God.

Will the body, then, stand alone without the Word, in an immortal and incorruptible state of irrationality and immobility? And how will the Word himself go into God and be joined to him again after his separation from the flesh? Was he not in God, then, when he was with the flesh? But he was in him always, being co-eternal and one and the same with God. How, then, was he in the body? If he dwelt in it as a soul does, then he will have his own subsistence, separate from the Father, living and subsisting in the flesh he assumed.

What, then, prevented confessing him as the living Son of God even before the foundation of the world? But perhaps he might say that he was present in the body by activity alone, and not by the subsistence of substance. For, he says, while he was with the flesh by effective activity alone (moving it and doing all the things recorded in the Gospels), he was joined in substance to God, as being his Word, inseparable and undivided from him.

If he says this, let him answer our question: did the activity of the Word reach this flesh alone, and not also other men, the saints of God? And is it not the same Word who acts in all the other works the Word has created? Indeed, we have learned that 'by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm,' and 'all things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being.' So he acts upon all things.

We know from the divine Scriptures also that 'the word of the Lord came to Hosea son of Beeri,' and 'the word of the Lord came to Isaiah son of Amoz,' and 'the word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah.' And in each of the prophets the same Word of God was at work. Did they all, then, share the same dignity as the only-begotten Son of God, and did the Savior have nothing more than they, if indeed he was moved only by the activity of the Word who is joined to God?

But Marcellus does not even allow the Christ of God an equal share with the prophets. For they will obtain eternal life, immortal and without end, living for all ages in the promised kingdom of heaven and enjoying good things 'which eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and which have not entered the heart of man.' But the Christ of God himself, the common Savior of all, 'the firstborn of the dead,' the hope of the saints' resurrection, will then be the only one left out: his kingdom will cease, and his life-giving flesh will be left bereft and without the Word. So, according to Marcellus's teaching, he neither existed beforehand as Son of God nor endures without end.

No wonder, then, that these things turned the truly God-loving and thrice-blessed emperor against the man, even though the man had flattered him endlessly and set out many praises of the emperor in his treatise. These same things forced the holy synod, which had gathered in the imperial city from various provinces (Pontus and Cappadocia, Asia, Phrygia and Bithynia, Thrace and the regions beyond), to denounce the man publicly in its document against him, even against its will. These things have also compelled us to take up the present examination, both in support of the decisions of the holy synod and to satisfy our fellow ministers, who instructed us to do this.

Above all, I consider this writing to have become necessary because of those who have thought the man was wronged. For we must heal our brothers' suspicion by bringing to light his unbelief toward the Son of God, which had long lurked within him but has now been exposed by his own writing. He brought that writing of his own accord, with no one summoning him, put it into the emperor's hands and asked him to judge its contents, perhaps hoping that in return for his praises of the emperor he would himself gain favor with him, while the bishops he had maligned would be punished.

But the outcome did not go as he had hoped. For God was the judge of these matters, and Christ Jesus himself, whom the writer had set at nought. He saw the man's hidden thoughts and arranged for him to become his own accuser and his own refutation, with no one forcing him. So the man came to the emperor priding himself on his treatise; the emperor handed the judgment of its contents over to the synod; and the holy synod of God rejected the writing, and rightly so, because it confesses neither a pious beginning nor a pious end for the Son of God.
